summary:
The longest contiguous stretch with at most two distinct values. Slide a window with a count per flavour and a
distinct counter; when a third flavour enters, advance the left edge until some flavour's count drops to
zero. O(n), with an array of counts since flavours are below `n`.

question.md:
Return the length of the longest run of consecutive tubs that uses at most two different flavours.

- **n up to 10⁵**, flavours in `[0, n)`.

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- One or two flavours in total: the whole counter.
- All tubs different: the answer is 2 (or 1 if there's a single tub).
- The best stretch may be in the middle; starting from the first tub isn't required.

think.md:
**Translating the story.** Starting anywhere and walking right until you can't continue means you take a
contiguous stretch of tubs. The cone allows two flavours, so the question is: the longest stretch with **at most
two distinct values**.

**Why the left edge never goes back.** If the window `[L, R]` breaks the rule, then every longer window `[L, R']` with
`R' > R` contains it and breaks the rule too. So once a start `L` fails for some `R`, it fails for all later `R`, and
we can throw it away forever. That's what lets the left pointer only move forward, and makes the whole scan O(n).

**Counting distinct values in O(1).** Keep a count per flavour and a separate number `distinct`. When a count goes
from 0 to 1, a new flavour entered (`distinct + 1`); when a count drops from 1 to 0, a flavour left completely
(`distinct − 1`). Other changes don't affect `distinct`.

When a third flavour enters, `L` must move until one of the flavours disappears entirely; that might take several
steps, because the leftmost tub's flavour may appear again later in the window.

idea.md: From every tub, walk right remembering at most two flavours; stop at the first tub whose flavour would be a third. Correct, but each start re-walks the same tubs.

lines.text: Take the tub if its flavour is one of the (up to) two already chosen, or a second one is still free.

notes.java: Flavours are non-negative, so `b = −1` means 'second flavour not chosen yet'.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²)**, e.g. for two alternating flavours. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: Start 0: the window grows to 0..2 (length 3). Adding 2 at 3 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 1: the window grows to 1..2 (length 2). Adding 2 at 3 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 2: the window grows to 2..6 (length 5). Adding 4 at 7 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 3: the window grows to 3..6 (length 4). Adding 4 at 7 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 4: the window grows to 4..6 (length 3). Adding 4 at 7 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Start 5: the window grows to 5..6 (length 2). Adding 4 at 7 would break the rule, so this start stops.
Starts 6..9 are checked the same way. The longest window starts at 2. In total about 39 cells were re-read, which grows like n²: the same cells are scanned again from every start.
Most scoops: 5.

walk.title: From each tub, walk until a third flavour appears.

limits.md: Re-walks the same tubs from every start.

approaches.title: Window with flavour counts

idea.md:
Sliding window with `count[f]` and `distinct`. Add `flavours[R]`; while `distinct > 2`, remove
`flavours[L]` and advance `L`. Record `R − L + 1`.

Because flavours are below `n`, a plain array of counts replaces a hash map.

**Generalises directly:** replace 2 by `k` for "longest stretch with at most `k` distinct values".

build: Add tub `R`: if its count goes 0 → 1, `distinct += 1`.

lines.text: Counts indexed by flavour (all flavours are below `n`), and the number of flavours present.
Add tub `i`; a flavour entering from zero is a new distinct one.
Three flavours: drop tubs from the left until a flavour disappears completely.

complexity.md: **Time O(n).** **Space O(n)** for the counts (a hash map would hold at most 3 keys).

steps.text: R adds 3 at 0; the rule still holds, so the window just grows to 0..0. New best: 1.
R adds 3 at 1; the rule still holds, so the window just grows to 0..1. New best: 2.
R adds 1 at 2; the rule still holds, so the window just grows to 0..2. New best: 3.
R adds 2 at 3. That breaks the rule (flavours [1, 2, 3]). L moves past 0..1 until it holds again: window 2..3.
R adds 1 at 4; the rule still holds, so the window just grows to 2..4.
R adds 1 at 5; the rule still holds, so the window just grows to 2..5. New best: 4.
R adds 2 at 6; the rule still holds, so the window just grows to 2..6. New best: 5.
R adds 4 at 7. That breaks the rule (flavours [1, 2, 4]). L moves past 2..5 until it holds again: window 6..7.
R adds 4 at 8; the rule still holds, so the window just grows to 6..8.
R adds 2 at 9; the rule still holds, so the window just grows to 6..9.
R visited each index once and L only ever moved right, so the pointers made at most 20 moves in total: O(n).
Most scoops: 5.

walk.title: Keep a count per flavour in the window and the number of distinct flavours. When a third flavour appears, drop tubs from the left until one flavour's count hits zero.

takeaways.md:
- **"At most k distinct values" windows:** counts + a distinct counter, updated only on 0 ↔ 1 transitions.
- Read the story carefully: "walk until you can't" means contiguous.
- Same template as every other longest-valid-window problem.
